summary: History/chronology topic for ages 9-11: build and order the key milestones of human space exploration and grasp the through-line from a competitive Space Race to a long-term, shared human presence in space. Anchor facts (who/what/roughly-when): Sputnik, first satellite, 1957 (Soviet); Yuri Gagarin, first human in space, 1961 (Soviet); Apollo 11, first crewed Moon landing, 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin (USA); then the Space Shuttle era, the International Space Station (permanently crewed international laboratory in low Earth orbit), and current directions — NASA's Artemis programme (returning humans to the Moon), Mars exploration, and commercial spaceflight (e.g. SpaceX). Current-programme details are live and change year to year, so teach them as still unfolding. Core goals: (1) name and order the firsts with roughly-right dates and people, and (2) see the arc from a USA-vs-USSR race for firsts to international and commercial cooperation.
misconceptions: Getting the order/agency wrong — e.g. thinking the USA launched the first satellite or put the first human in space, when those firsts (Sputnik, Gagarin) were Soviet.
Thinking humans have landed on Mars, or currently live on the Moon, rather than the Moon landings being Apollo-era and today's crews living on the ISS in low Earth orbit.
Believing space exploration stopped after Apollo, missing the Shuttle era, the ISS, and current Artemis/commercial activity.
Conflating satellites, crewed missions, and robotic probes as the same thing.
Assuming only one country/agency does spaceflight, overlooking international (ISS) and commercial (SpaceX) participation.
Treating current-programme details as fixed facts when they are live and change year to year.

activities.title: Build the space-exploration timeline
steps: Lay out a horizontal timeline and place each milestone in order from left to right by when it began: 1957 Sputnik → 1961 Gagarin → 1969 Apollo 11 → Space Shuttle era (1981–2011) → International Space Station (crewed since 2000, still in use) → present-day Artemis/commercial spaceflight. Note that the Shuttle era and the ISS overlapped: Shuttles helped build the ISS.

For each milestone state WHO, WHAT and ROUGHLY WHEN in your own words: Sputnik = first satellite, 1957; Gagarin = first human in space, 1961; Apollo 11 = first crewed Moon landing, 1969 with Armstrong and Aldrin.
Use two colours (or two strands) to track the Space Race back-and-forth: mark which firsts were Soviet (Sputnik, Gagarin) and which was the USA (first people on the Moon).
Mark a 'you are here' node at the present end and label it 'still being written' to show today's chapter is ongoing.
Explain the arc aloud: a tense Cold-War race for firsts between the USA and USSR gave way to living and working in space and to international + commercial cooperation.
activities.insight: The events form an ordered story with causes, not a scatter of facts: competition drove rapid firsts, which gave way to a shared, continuing human presence in space.

activities.title: Lift-the-flap: who got there first?
steps: Before revealing the answer, predict which country achieved each first: the first satellite, the first human in space, the first crewed Moon landing.
Reveal each answer and check your prediction: first satellite (Sputnik) and first human (Gagarin) were Soviet; first Moon landing (Apollo 11) was the USA.
Say in one sentence why reaching the Moon first does NOT mean the USA led at every step.
activities.insight: Whoever reached the Moon first was not first at everything: during the Space Race the firsts were shared between the two sides — the Soviet Union led early (first satellite 1957, first human 1961) and the USA was first to land people on the Moon (1969).

activities.title: Then and now: a living, ongoing story
steps: Pair a past achievement with its present-day counterpart, e.g. Apollo's single-use Saturn V rocket vs a modern reusable rocket, or a single Moon mission vs people living on the ISS right now.

Name at least one current space effort — the International Space Station, NASA's Artemis programme, or a commercial company such as SpaceX — and describe its goal in a sentence (e.g. Artemis aims to return humans to the Moon).
State clearly what is true TODAY: no human has set foot on Mars; nobody lives on the Moon now; astronauts currently live and work on the ISS orbiting Earth.
Note which current details might change (planned dates, upcoming missions) and mark them as still unfolding rather than fixed facts.
activities.insight: Space exploration did not end with Apollo; it continues now through the ISS, Artemis and commercial spaceflight, and today's plans are live and subject to change.

activities.title: Talk to someone who was there
steps: Take on, or interview, an in-role figure from a milestone — for example an Apollo astronaut recalling standing on the Moon in 1969, or a mission controller during Gagarin's or Sputnik's launch.
Ask 'what was it like to be first?' and have the figure answer while keeping the historical facts (who, what, year) honest.
After the conversation, place that figure's event correctly on the timeline with its date.
activities.insight: The milestones are human stories; stepping into a first-person account is intended to make the chronology feel more vivid, while the date, people and 'first' claim must still match the real record.

activities.title: Order-and-match check
steps: Put a shuffled set of milestones (Apollo 11, Sputnik, the ISS, Gagarin's flight) into chronological order.

Match each event to its rough year and, where there is one, its key person (e.g. Gagarin's flight – Yuri Gagarin; Apollo 11 – Armstrong and Aldrin); note that Sputnik carried no people and the ISS has had many crews, not one person.
Answer which country achieved a given first (e.g. first satellite, first human, first Moon landing).
activities.insight: You can independently recall and order the milestones and attribute each first to the right country, confirming the chronology stuck.

checkQuestion: The United States landed the first people on the Moon in 1969. Does that mean the USA was also first to launch a satellite and first to send a human into space — or was it another country? Tell me WHO did what, and roughly WHEN.
checkAnswer: No — the USA was first to land people on the Moon (Apollo 11, 1969, with Armstrong and Aldrin), but it was NOT first into space. The Soviet Union (Russia) got there first: it launched the first satellite, Sputnik, in 1957, and sent the first human, Yuri Gagarin, into space in 1961. That competition between the two countries was called the Space Race. Since then came the Space Shuttle era, the International Space Station where astronauts live and work today, and current efforts like NASA's Artemis programme (returning to the Moon) and commercial companies such as SpaceX.
